name: Carla Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by checking the tool box and the cutting list, then help set doors or patch the timber work wherever the forewoman needs me. I came into construction only recently after years cleaning offices, so at fifty-eight I still ask twice before making a cut. My partner Anton makes tea while I pack boots, and our grown daughter phones on Sundays. I like seeing a door close cleanly; climbing and rushed measurements are the rough part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little software that saves checking time is fine if the crew still gets proper hours. I sometimes use a phone tool to turn my rough measurements into a neat list, but I check every number with a tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my pay is sound while the Oak Street renovation stays busy, but I don't have a lifetime of trade contacts. Anton's shop hours vary by season, so our four months of savings never feels as large as it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep making doors and patching timber, and I'll keep double-checking the phone list against the tape. In the first year I'd put the same fixed amount into our savings account each payday, while asking forewoman Leena about the next site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about this one, yet Anton's short winter hours make me watch our cash. Software isn't the thing that wakes me; a blank week on the work board is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the phone list if the tool saves time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once typed 180 instead of 108 and noticed only when the door lining looked wrong. A screen can make a mistake look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a blank week on the board mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use savings for the rent and groceries, then I'd phone the two builders Leena has named. Our daughter is settled elsewhere and shouldn't be drawn into our ordinary bills.

say: I'd welcome a **neater cutting list** if crew hours remain stable.
I'd still check every **phone measurement** against a tape.
think: My pay is sound on the **Oak Street** renovation, but I lack long trade contacts.
Anton's **seasonal hours** keep our four-month cushion on my mind.
do: Keep setting **doors** and checking the phone list with a tape.
Deposit the **usual amount** each payday and ask about the next site.
feel: **Steady** about small software changes, with winter cash still in view.
S0.quote: A screen can make a mistake look tidy.
fieldNote: Carla's occasional phone tool use is bounded by a remembered **measurement error** and a habit of physical checking.
The household's **four-month reserve** has to absorb Anton's seasonal shop hours as well as any construction gap.

steps.text: Keep setting doors on the Oak Street renovation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the others that a computer can buy hinges, but the door still has to hang straight. I'd ask Leena to show us any new ordering tool before we lose time fixing its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our office will need fewer people for orders and estimates, and that could leave the crews waiting between jobs. My own hands are useful, though I'm junior and the small builders nearby will all be chasing the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Leena for the forward work board and sit with the ordering clerk when the new system is tried. If it's still useful after a month, I'll learn the parts that make our cutting lists clearer; if site hours dip, Anton and I will stop eating out on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert rather than defeated, because I can learn a tool when it proves itself. The worry is a missing contract, especially when Anton's winter shop hours are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the clerk to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see how it counts hinges and flags a late delivery, since those mistakes hold up the whole doorway. I don't need its sales pitch; I need one good job done with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you volunteer to be the first to use a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch a real order first, then take my turn with the clerk beside me. I've learned enough new tools to know rushing the first day is poor sense.

say: I'd say **hinges** can be ordered by software while doors still need skilled hands.
I'd ask for a **real demonstration** before the crew relies on new ordering.
think: Fewer office staff could mean **gaps between contracts** for site crews.
My **junior standing** leaves fewer local openings if builders slow hiring.
do: Check Leena's **forward work board** and observe an actual order.
Learn the **ordering tool** after a successful month of use.
Stop **Friday meals out** if site hours dip.
feel: **Alert** and willing to learn, with household hours still uncertain.
S1.quote: I don't need its sales pitch; I need one good job done with it.
fieldNote: Her acceptance of software depends on a **working order** and delivery, fitting her habit of testing claims on site.
The private risk is not the door task itself but fewer contracts and Anton's existing **seasonal hours**.

steps.text: Learn the ordering tool after a month of successful site use
Stop Friday meals out if site hours fall
Keep hanging doors while the contract continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the tool shed I'd say we should get the current doors finished before anybody writes us off. I'd also remind Leena that a thinking machine in 2028 and site robots in 2031 are two different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the thinking work can be done cheaper, and the estimates and orders may change immediately. At sixty-three, capable robots could do the door fitting too; with Anton's uneven shop hours, I couldn't simply declare retirement and stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll ask Leena to let me practise the site ordering tool and put an extra small amount in savings after full weeks. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid door work while it exists, then apply to two building-maintenance teams if the site book starts thinning; I would check their real vacancies before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened by how little time two years is, but I haven't run out of moves. I would need the family bills written down before I could judge how much work I must keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anton tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Anton we need to see what our four-month cushion actually buys if either wage falls. I'd ask him to keep the shop rota slips so we can count the short weeks honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building maintenance if robots can also do hands-on tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maintenance might give me paid time before robots reach site work, and older buildings need odd repairs. I don't claim building-maintenance work would be safe after 2031; I'd apply only where the vacancy and pay are real.

say: I'd tell the crew to **finish current doors** while work is there.
I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from hands-on robots around 2031.
think: At **sixty**, office estimates and orders could change before site fitting does.
At **sixty-three**, robots could replace fitting while Anton's shop wages remain uneven.
do: Practise the **ordering tool** and save extra after full weeks.
Keep **paid door work** in 2029 while it exists.
Apply for **building maintenance** if the site book thins.
feel: **Frightened by speed**, but still able to plan and check vacancies.
S2.quote: I don't claim building-maintenance work would be safe after 2031; I'd apply only where the vacancy and pay are real.
fieldNote: Carla marks the **three-year gap** between office disruption and site robots, without treating maintenance as permanently protected.
She wants **real vacancy** and wage evidence before moving, and Anton's rota slips before estimating household risk.

steps.text: Practise the site ordering tool with Leena
Add extra savings after full site weeks
Keep taking paid door work in 2029
Apply to two maintenance teams if site bookings thin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us judge tools by what they do on a real renovation. I would ask the firm to show its plans while there is still time to move workers between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three the office work could go to AI; by sixty-six, the robot could set doors as well as I do. I might be ready to stop then, but that's a decision for Anton and me with figures on the table, not a guess about a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll keep learning the site ordering tool and ask Leena to let me practise repairs on older door frames. In 2032 I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts if offered and check actual maintenance openings; before 2034, Anton and I will review savings and shop income to decide whether shorter hours are affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel I can use the extra years, although I don't enjoy picturing a machine doing a whole doorway. I'd rather have a choice based on a real bank balance than a brave story told over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by practising repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old frames are rarely square, and I need more practice trimming a jamb without wasting timber. Leena can watch the first few; those paid tasks teach me more than a glossy brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek a formal trade course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a local course included paid placement, I'd consider enrolling, but I won't pay a fee on a maybe. Anton and I need wages now and a clear reason to change trades.

say: I'd say five years allows **real site trials** before decisions are made.
I'd ask the firm for **worker plans** while moves are still possible.
think: I may need fitting wages at **sixty-three** even after AI changes office work.
At **sixty-six**, retirement depends on actual household figures, not assumed pension money.
do: Practise **older-frame repairs** and the site ordering tool.
Keep **paid fitting shifts** in 2032 and inspect maintenance vacancies.
Review **savings and shop income** before considering shorter hours.
feel: **Some control** from extra time, alongside discomfort about full robot fitting.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a choice based on a real bank balance than a brave story told over lunch.
fieldNote: Carla uses **five years** to deepen paid repair skills and test the household budget rather than announce retirement.
Her conditional interest in a course depends on **paid placement**, which she has not secured or planned to enrol in.

steps.text: Learn the site ordering tool through actual orders
Keep taking paid fitting shifts in 2032
Check maintenance openings before site bookings fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my neighbours ten years is a long stretch of workdays and none of us knows what a site will look like then. I would keep training my eye and hands on the jobs in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I hope Anton and I can choose fewer hours by then, but his shop income and our savings will decide whether I still need paid repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working and build our savings after full weeks, with Anton and me checking the totals each winter. In 2037, if I still need income, I'd take paid repair calls and use the ordering tool only for the jobs where it has proved accurate; before the 2039 robot date we'd revisit whether the work remains worth the strain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about what can change over a decade, and calmer about the machine dates. I am still careful with money because Anton's seasonal hours and my knees belong to the present, not to 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reduce hours before 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real stretch of full earnings and a safe savings figure could let me drop the heaviest site days. If the figures are poor, I'd keep paid lighter repairs as long as my body allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might your daughter do in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can visit and eat with us; she doesn't need to fund us. I wouldn't build a retirement plan on our grown daughter's wages.

say: I'd say **ten years** contains many workdays we can still use.
I'd keep my **hands and eye** trained on current site jobs.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid repairs may still be needed after thinking AI arrives.
At **seventy-one**, savings and Anton's wages determine whether I can stop before robots spread.
do: Keep **paid work** and save extra after full weeks.
Take **repair calls** in 2037 if household income requires them.
Review **site strain** and finances before the 2039 robot date.
feel: More **curious and calm** about distant machines, though present income remains uncertain.
S4.quote: I wouldn't build a retirement plan on our grown daughter's wages.
fieldNote: The **long timeline** shifts her focus to earned savings and lighter paid repairs, without assuming she can retire.
Anton's **seasonal shop hours** and her physical limits keep household income unsettled even before technology changes.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site and repair work while fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because the dates crowd my sixtieth birthday and I still need wages. A clear site schedule, real maintenance vacancies and a chance to learn the ordering tool on paid time would help; I need facts I can test, not a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks a tool's mistakes. If I cut timber from the wrong number, I pay with time and material, so a person must still check the measurement even when the order looks tidy.

headlineQuote: Software isn't the thing that wakes me; a blank week on the work board is.
portrait: Carla is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** site worker who entered carpentry after cleaning offices.
She uses a **phone tool** occasionally but verifies measurements against her tape.
Her four-month cushion supports two earners whose **hours vary**, so contract gaps already matter.
She seeks **tested tools**, paid repair practice and real vacancies before making a job move.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** compresses her earning window before capable site robots could arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **clear site schedule**, real maintenance vacancies and paid time to learn ordering software.
